Honey bees show strong flower constancy and often stick to one species on a foraging trip, but mixed trips are common enough that the absolute rule fails.
Human multiple births of six, seven, eight and nine are well documented, so five is not the maximum.
Age polyethism runs the other way: young bees work in the hive and older bees forage, and foragers become worn and less hairy, not smoother.
Most bony fishes have an operculum and sharks and rays have naked gill slits, but cartilaginous chimaeras have an operculum, so cartilage does not explain the absence.
Nearly all living horned mammals are cloven-hoofed bovids, and solid-hoofed equids are unhorned; rhinos are odd-toed and their horns are not a lateral pair.
Dolphins are viviparous and have two inguinal mammary glands opening as slits beside the genital opening, from which milk is ejected without projecting teats.
In nearly all insects the male intromittent organ enters the female; a few groups have unusual coupling, but the reverse is not the general pattern.
Hairy mammals are almost all live-bearing, but echidnas have hair and spines and lay eggs, as does the platypus.
Elephant pregnancy lasts about 18 to 22 months, near two years, and single calves are the rule, with twins very rare.
In sheatfish such as Silurus the male guards the nest and fry after the female leaves, though guarding for a full forty or fifty days is longer than typical hatching care.
Eels do not arise by spontaneous generation; freshwater eels develop from eggs spawned at sea and return as larvae.
Cicada song is produced by male tymbals; females of both large and small species lack that organ and are effectively silent.
Rabies is a fatal neurological infection of dogs and is transmitted by bites, but transmission is not certain on every bite and untreated humans die of it as well.
Hair follicles stop producing hair at death; the apparent lengthening is skin shrinkage exposing stubble.
Men, sheep, goats and pigs have the same dental counts in both sexes; male pigs have larger canines, not more teeth.
Many hybrids besides mules are sterile or sterile in one sex, and some hybrids, such as wolf-dogs, are fertile, so mules are not the unique exception.
Sperm carries a germline genome, not material drawn from every organ; inheritance of acquired body parts in the semen is not how heredity works.
Partridges and many other ground birds use a broken-wing distraction display to lead a predator from the brood, then return and call the young.
Most broadcast-spawning fishes lose the great majority of eggs before or soon after hatching, and high fecundity compensates for that mortality.
Octopuses have eight arms, but squid and cuttlefish add two long tentacles and the chambered nautilus has dozens of appendages, so not all cephalopods have eight feet.
Female brown and black bears give birth in the winter den, fast while concealed, and bring cubs out around early spring; tropical bears do not follow this pattern.
Many scaly bony fishes bear live young, many sharks and skates lay egg cases, and the angler is a bony fish rather than the sole exception among cartilaginous fishes.
Eels are oviparous and spawn after a breeding migration; their gonads and genital ducts exist but mature at sea, which is why they were long missed in fresh water.
Some sharks form a yolk-sac placenta after the yolk is used, so the embryo stays in the uterus and is nourished by the mother.
Humans and horses do grey with age, but so do dogs, wolves and several other mammals, so the near-uniqueness fails.
The argonaut's arm web secretes and holds its shell; it does not raise that web as a sail or trail arms as oars.
Solitary spider-hunting wasps paralyse spiders, seal them in mud cells, and lay an egg from which a wasp develops; that matches the described life history.
The human thorax normally has twelve pairs of ribs, not eight.
Partridges are impregnated by copulation; wind, voice or breath does not fertilise the female.
Kidney position varies, and in humans the right kidney sits lower than the left because of the liver, so the universal claim is false.
The hive's reproductive female lays the eggs that become both new queens and workers, the caste depending on how the larva is fed.
Some swans are vocal, but they do not sing chiefly when dying or fly out to sea to die.
The trunk is an elongated nose, and swimming elephants raise it above the surface and breathe through it.
Humans have a very high encephalisation quotient, but several small mammals and birds have larger brains relative to body mass, and brains are not uniquely moist.
In temperate social wasps the workers die at the end of the season and mated queens overwinter in sheltered holes; some tropical colonies persist longer.
Female octopuses guard their eggs and typically stop feeding, lose condition and die around the time the eggs hatch.
A honey-bee worker's barbed sting often tears out with the venom apparatus when it stings elastic skin, and that injury is fatal, but bees can sting other insects without dying.
Crocodiles depress the lower jaw like other vertebrates; the upper jaw is part of the skull, and only the whole head lifts at the neck.
Crabs, crayfish and lobsters moult repeatedly through life and are soft until the new cuticle hardens.
Grey mullet move from the sea into estuaries, marshes and rivers to feed, and anguillid eels leave fresh water and migrate to the sea to spawn.
Scorpion young ride on the mother and do not kill her; only a minority of spiders let the brood consume the mother.
Temperate snakes and lizards often brumate in winter and fast, but the fixed four-month fast does not hold for river crocodiles in warm climates or for all populations.
Oysters, cockles, limpets and barnacles do favour different substrates, but they arise from eggs and larvae, not spontaneous generation in mud.
Lice infest many birds and mammals, but not every individual, and donkeys have both lice and ticks.
The brain is richly supplied with blood vessels and, in living animals, is warm and metabolically active, not bloodless and cold.
Most raptors hunt alone or in pairs, but vultures, some kites and several falcons gather, roost or nest in groups.
Swallows, storks, turtle-doves and kites migrate rather than overwinter naked in holes; true hibernation is known in only a few birds such as the poorwill.
Most fishes have separate sexes, and some sea basses are simultaneous hermaphrodites that always carry eggs, but it is not established that both named kinds are never found without eggs.
Cuckoos are not hawks: their feet are not raptorial talons and they are a separate lineage, though hawks do sometimes kill other birds of prey.
Many light-eyed babies are born with blue-grey irises that later darken, but many children are born with dark eyes, and eye colour can change in other mammals.
Horned bovids lack upper incisors, have a four-chambered stomach and chew the cud, but camels and chevrotains also ruminate and are not horned animals of that type.
Offspring usually resemble parents, and recessive and other inherited traits can skip a generation and reappear in a grandchild.
Sensation is processed in the brain; brain tissue itself has little pain sensation, but the heart is not the sensory centre.
The male octopus's specialised arm transfers spermatophores into the female and is a reproductive organ, not merely an attachment.
Elephants usually live shorter lives than people, and tortoises, bowhead whales and some sharks and clams live longer than humans.
Pigeons are socially monogamous and pairs often last until a mate dies, while extra-pair mating by females does occur.
Living horned bovids lack tusks and typical carnivore dentitions lack horns, but deer such as muntjacs combine antlers with elongated canine tusks.
Most birds, including the common kingfisher, breed in spring and summer; kingfishers do not nest at the winter solstice.
Sessile molluscs, barnacles and limpets reproduce sexually, whether as separate sexes or hermaphrodites, and many plants have separate sexes as well.
Electric rays stun prey with discharges from organs in the body and can deliver a shock strong enough to numb a person.
Individual fishes do get sick, and epidemic diseases of fishes, including viral haemorrhagic and herpesvirus outbreaks, are well known.
Fig wasps develop in caprifigs, enter the cultivated fig and pollinate it so the fruit sets, which is why growers hang wild figs in the trees.
Caponizing an adult cock shrinks and pales the comb and reduces crowing and mating drive; castration before puberty prevents those male traits from developing.
Crocodiles gape and small birds forage near them, but regular, tolerated tooth-cleaning inside the mouth is not securely established.
Cuckoos build no nest and usually lay one egg in a smaller bird's nest, and the host rears the chick, but the female typically removes one egg while the chick, not the adult, destroys the rest.
Male sharks and dogfish have paired claspers beside the cloaca, and females do not; the difference holds across these fishes.
Crocodiles often stay in water at night, and water can be warmer than night air, but they also come ashore and the thermal explanation is only part of the pattern.
Bees secrete wax from abdominal glands and make honey by processing floral nectar; honey is not dew gathered ready-made from the air.
Boys castrated before puberty do not develop a beard or a broken voice, and without adult androgens they do not develop male-pattern baldness.
Embryonic organs appear in sequence; they are not all present in miniature from the start.
Many mobile animals, including snails, earthworms and some fishes, are hermaphrodites, and many plants have separate male and female individuals.
Smooth-hound sharks nourish embryos through a yolk-sac connection to the uterine wall after the yolk is used, with extraembryonic membranes analogous to those of mammals.
Fishes have eyes, but they also have olfactory organs opening by nostrils and inner ears with otoliths, even though they lack external ears.
Some congenital defects are heritable, but lameness, blindness from injury, scars and pimples acquired in life are not passed to children.
In most insect species females are larger than males because of fecundity selection, though males are larger in some groups.
Bird sex is set by sex chromosomes at fertilisation, not by whether the egg is long or round.
In clawed lobsters either side may carry the crusher claw, but crabs and crayfish are not invariably right-clawed, and spiny lobsters lack that claw asymmetry.
Dog pregnancy is usually about 63 days and often falls between 60 and 63 from ovulation, but litters born a little earlier than 60 days from mating can survive.
Hyenas are not hermaphrodites; each animal is one sex, and both sexes have a pouch under the tail that helped create the contrary impression.
Human semen is whitish or greyish in every population and is not black.
Many mammals turn head-down before birth and are born head first, but orientation is not universal early on, and whales and dolphins are normally born tail first.
Dolphins, whales and other cetaceans breathe by a blowhole and are placental mammals that bear live young rather than laying eggs.
Octopuses match the colour and pattern of nearby stones both while hunting and when threatened.
The lion's neck is a chain of cervical vertebrae, as in other mammals, not a single bone.
Large birds often delay breeding, but most bird species are small songbirds that breed in their first year.
A breeding pair of eagles holds a large territory and drives off its independent young and other eagles, but it does not exclude all other birds.
In the bird egg the embryonic heart appears early as a pulsing point of blood, with paired vessels running from it over the yolk.
Common cranes breed on Eurasian steppes and many winter in Nile-basin marshes of Sudan and Ethiopia.
Bees do not pick up stones to ballast themselves in wind.
Females are larger than males in many sharks and in a majority of other fishes, though male-larger species are numerous.
Boys commonly begin producing semen around fourteen, but they can father children in the mid-teens, not only from about twenty-one.
Hens and geese that have never mated still lay unfertilised eggs, so those eggs are not leftovers of an earlier mating.
Offspring of injured parents are not born with those injuries, and children are often unlike their parents in many traits.
Dogs, lions, wolves, foxes and jackals are born with sealed eyelids, but not every many-toed quadruped is; hyenas, for example, are born with open eyes.
Caterpillars feed and defecate, while the chrysalis does neither, and the same feeding arrest holds for the pupae of bees, wasps and other insects that pupate.
Men and women have the same cranial sutures; sex does not replace three meeting sutures with one circular suture.
Across animals, larger species tend to have fewer offspring and smaller ones more, though bats, many fishes and other groups break the pattern.
The angler lies buried in sediment and twitches a slender lure with a fleshy tip in front of the mouth to draw small fish within striking range.
Some sharks, rays and bony fishes give birth to live young while breathing water, so air-breathing is not required for internal viviparity.
In vertebrate embryos the heart is among the first organs to form and beat and it connects to early vessels, but it is not the origin of the other body parts.
Human laughter is distinctive, but apes produce laughter-like calls and rats vocalise when tickled, so neither laughter nor ticklishness is unique to humans.
